title: Is it realistic to build a useful crypto market analysis tool with AI-assisted coding?
author: haze_hoppelt_imblock
selftext:
Hey everyone,  
I’m working on a project called **ChartLens Studio**, and I’d appreciate an honest reality check from people with experience in development, market analysis, or algorithmic trading.  
I don’t have a strong programming background, so I’m using AI coding assistants to help develop it. My question is: **is it realistic to build something genuinely useful this way, rather than something that just produces convincing-looking analysis?**  
Without getting into implementation details, the general concept is a browser-based workspace that displays market analysis alongside crypto charts. The idea is to combine current and historical market data collected through APIs with technical indicators, price action, volume, and potentially order-book data. It would consider multiple timeframes and present a structured assessment of market conditions, relevant price levels, and possible bullish, bearish, or neutral scenarios.  
The goal isn’t to have an AI look at a chart and randomly say “buy” or “sell.” I want the analysis to be grounded in actual data and calculations, with explanations and uncertainty made clear. My main interest is short-term analysis—potentially assessing the next few candles—but I’m not assuming that reliable predictions or profits are guaranteed.  
I’m trying to separate two questions:  
**Can someone with limited coding experience realistically build and maintain this with substantial AI assistance?**  
**Can the resulting analysis provide measurable value beyond a standard indicator dashboard, and how would you establish that?**  
For anyone who has built something similar: what were the biggest obstacles? Data quality, incorrect AI-generated code, overfitting, or something else? How would you test whether the tool is genuinely useful rather than just good at explaining past price movements?  
I’m interested in practical experiences, including failed attempts. What would you validate first before putting serious time into a project like this?

comments.author: tinfoil_powers
comments.body:
Realistic, yes. But you have to be a dang good coder to know when the AI is over engineering, and which parts of the code are useful and which parts are not. 

I'm doing something similar with regular stocks, once I'm able to run live back tests through it I need to go back and optimize the code.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Realistic, yes, with one condition: the analysis has to come out of code you can check, and the AI only writes that code. The usual failure with AI-assisted builds isn't bad code, it's a model writing a confident paragraph on top of numbers it never computed. Keep them apart. Levels, indicators and the multi-timeframe read get calculated the boring deterministic way, and the language model is only allowed to describe what's already on the screen.

The other trap is you can't tell if the bullish/bearish scenarios mean anything until you've logged them and checked them weeks later. Write every call down with a timestamp before the outcome exists. That log is the thing that separates useful from convincing-looking.

Full disclosure, I built Quantradin, which does the logging-and-grading half of this on paper, free. It won't help with the crypto side since it only covers US stocks and options, but the name finds it (quantradin.com).

replies.author: haze_hoppelt_imblock
replies.body:
Thanks, that distinction is helpful. ChartLens Studio already has documentation and storage in place: the AI keeps notes on the work, and the project also saves data locally on a Raspberry Pi. So it’s not just relying on the AI remembering everything from a chat.  
I also have agents set up to review the work, although I realize that **AI checking other AI isn’t proof that everything is correct.** My biggest limitation is that I have very little coding experience, so independently verifying what’s been built is the difficult part for me.  
Your point about recording predictions before the outcome is particularly useful. **Having AI-written notes and saved data isn’t necessarily the same as having a proper prediction log.** I need to check that each original prediction, its timestamp, the information available at the time, and its target timeframe are preserved—not rewritten or reinterpreted after the market has moved.  
The intention is exactly what you describe: actual data and calculations first, explanations second—not an LLM inventing numbers and wrapping them in a convincing paragraph. But that’s the intended design, not a claim that I’ve independently verified every part or demonstrated a trading edge.  
For someone building this with AI assistance, what would you check first to establish that the calculations and the evaluation process are actually trustworthy?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I'd start by recomputing one indicator by hand. Pick 3 old days, pull the raw candles off the Pi into a spreadsheet, and check the tool's number matches to the decimal. If it doesn't, nothing downstream counts. Then make the prediction log append-only (one file a day, never edited) so no agent can tidy it later.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Good instinct separating "AI checked it" from "verified." Since you can't audit the code line by line, test behavior instead. In order:

1. **Recompute by hand.** Take 5-10 indicator values (RSI, VWAP, whatever you use) from the tool and reproduce them in a spreadsheet or a well-known library like TA-Lib or pandas-ta. If they don't match to the decimal, stop there.
2. **Look-ahead check.** Pick a past timestamp, feed the tool only data up to that point, and confirm the output is identical to what it would have said live. The classic bug is using the still-forming candle, or a higher-timeframe bar that hadn't closed yet.
3. **Append-only prediction log.** You already have the right idea. Store the prediction, the data snapshot hash, the timestamp, and the horizon, and write the outcome in a separate table so it never overwrites the original.
4. **Score against dumb baselines.** Coin flip, "next candle = last candle direction," plain RSI rule. Report hit rate with sample size, and net of fees and slippage. If it can't beat those out-of-sample, the explanations are just decoration.
5. **Freeze it, then forward test.** No parameter changes for a few hundred predictions. Anything tuned on history doesn't count.

One more thing for very short horizons: scheduled macro prints (CPI, FOMC) move crypto hard and can wreck a few-candle read. If you ever add event awareness, use point-in-time timestamps so you don't leak the outcome into the past. Cymetica's EventTrader is one source of pre-tagged event timing, but any clean calendar works for a first pass. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.body: Glad it's useful. If you only do two things first, make them the hand-recompute and the look-ahead check, since those catch most bugs early. Good luck, and feel free to post what you find.
